title: Lois “Princess Nowedonah” Hunter
summary: Lois Marie Hunter, also known as Princess Nowedonah, was a Shinnecock educator, author, public speaker, and tribal historian whose work taught Shinnecock continuity, public memory, women's advocacy, and Native self-representation in the 20th century.
content:
Lois Marie Hunter (1903-1975), known publicly as Princess Nowedonah, was a Shinnecock educator, author, public speaker, and tribal historian. Her life helps show Native Long Island history as a continuing community story carried by teachers, writers, families, public gatherings, and Shinnecock memory.

Hunter was the daughter of Lulu and Charles Hunter and the granddaughter of Wickham Cuffee, a Shinnecock figure remembered in community history and public collections. She spent much of her life on the Shinnecock Indian Reservation and became one of the 20th-century voices through whom Shinnecock people explained their own history, cultural pride, and continued presence.

Education and Teaching

Hunter attended Shinnecock community schools and graduated from Cheyney State Teachers College in Pennsylvania. After completing her formal education, she returned home and taught at the Shinnecock Reservation School before World War II.

That return matters because Hunter's education was not separated from community responsibility. She brought her training back into a setting where Shinnecock children could learn from a Shinnecock teacher who understood local history, family relationships, and the importance of Native self-representation.

Writer and Tribal Historian

Hunter wrote The Shinnecock Indians, a short history of her people that circulated in the mid-20th century. Sources cite the publication with conflicting dates, so the safest public framing is that the work belongs to her broader mid-century effort to teach Shinnecock history from a Native perspective.

Her writing and lectures were important at a time when many local histories treated Native people as vanished, archaeological, or only visible through colonial records. Hunter's work kept Shinnecock memory, lineage, and public identity in Shinnecock hands.

Public Speaking and Storytelling

Princess Nowedonah presented Shinnecock history, stories, and cultural knowledge in public settings, including schools, churches, community programs, and intertribal gatherings. Her public teaching should be understood as education and survivance: she translated parts of community history for broader audiences while also insisting that outsiders respect Shinnecock privacy and self-determination.

Sources also describe Hunter as protective of Shinnecock community boundaries. In an interview context cited by Gaynell Stone, she pushed back against outsiders who claimed to know the Shinnecock simply by visiting or studying them, making clear that Native people had the right to speak for themselves and to be left alone when they chose.

Church and Community Life

Hunter was active in Shinnecock church and community life. Public sources connect her work to Shinnecock Presbyterian Church, the Reservation School, tribal history, and community programs, but they do not clearly identify her with a formal church office. For that reason, it is most accurate to describe her as active in church and community life rather than naming a formal church office.

In 1939, Hunter and Abigail Fithian Halsey helped create the Heady Creek Shinnecock Pageant to raise funds after the Shinnecock Presbyterian Church was damaged by the Hurricane of 1938. From 1940 to 1943, Hunter and the Shinnecock community repeated the pageant to continue the historical dramatization and support the church.

Powwow Voice

At the Shinnecock Powwow, Princess Nowedonah made opening addresses before her death. Her 1972 address, delivered on her sixty-ninth birthday, welcomed visitors while reminding them they were standing on Shinnecock land and that the public owed an ongoing debt of respect to Native people.

Her Powwow presence connected hospitality, intertribal solidarity, public education, and Shinnecock sovereignty in one public setting. She also commented on Shinnecock women's regalia and Algonquian design knowledge, showing how public celebration and careful cultural memory could exist together.

Women's Political Advocacy

Hunter was part of Shinnecock women's advocacy for political rights within tribal governance. In 1967, Lois Hunter and Harriett Crippen Gumbs, also known as Starleaf, raised the issue of Shinnecock women's voting rights in tribal trustee elections, and Hunter testified before the Suffolk County Human Rights Commission.

The issue was not resolved immediately. Later changes came through continued community work in the 1990s, but Hunter's testimony stands as an important public moment in the longer history of Shinnecock women's political agency and the effort to restore roles that had been constrained by colonial governance structures.

Legacy

When Hunter died in 1975, John A. Strong later described her funeral as a visible moment in Shinnecock cultural reaffirmation. After a Christian service at the reservation church, younger Shinnecock people incorporated Native drumming and singing into the public procession.

The importance of that moment is not in disclosing private ceremony, but in understanding how Hunter's lifetime of teaching helped younger generations express Native pride in public community life. Her biography connects Shinnecock history to education, writing, women's advocacy, Powwow addresses, church life, and the right of Native people to define their own history.

Oral Stories

Princess Nowedonah's oral story The Story of Poggatatuck and Ashwa: The Enchanted Spring is preserved in a public recording and connects her educational work with Eastern Long Island story traditions.

The 1950 Book

Hunter framed The Shinnecock Indians as a walk through ancestral ground and a record of knowledge carried by Shinnecock families. Published in 1950, the book is an early Shinnecock-authored community history that places living memory beside documentary history and rejects the idea that Native Long Island belongs only to the past.

References

  • Beverly Jensen, Shinnecock Indian Nation, 2015.
  • Gaynell Stone, The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History, 1983.
  • Lois Marie Hunter, The Shinnecock Indians (Buys Bros., 1950), PDF p. 5 (book p. IX).
  • Harvey G. Laudin, The Shinnecock Powwow, in Shinnecock cultural-history source collections.
  • John A. Strong, We Are Still Here! The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island Today, 1998.
  • John A. Strong, The Reaffirmation of Tradition Among the Native Americans of Eastern Long Island, Long Island Historical Journal, Vol. 7, No. 1, Fall 1994.
  • Nancy Shoemaker, ed., Living with Whales: Documents and Oral Histories of Native New England Whaling History, 2014.
why_this_matters: Lois Hunter's story centers Shinnecock women's leadership, education, writing, and public advocacy. Her biography shows Native cultural authority and community knowledge in the 20th century, especially the ways Shinnecock people taught and defended their own history.
activity_update_summary: Expanded Lois Hunter's biography with material from her 1950 book and stronger connections to her teaching, public history, and community work.
